claim: The medial prefrontal cortex plays a central role in social behavior.
source: The medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) plays a central role in social behavior (Duncan and Owen, 2000; Wood and Grafman, 2003; Bicks et al., 2015) through functional interactions with the amygdala (Kumar et al., 2014; Adhikari et al., 2015; Bukalo et al., 2015; Tovote et al., 2015), a region that is reciprocally connected with the mPFC (Vertes, 2004; Hoover and Vertes, 2007; Adhikari et al., 2015) and plays central roles in emotional responses such as fear and anxiety.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research establishing this relationship

claim: The medial prefrontal cortex functions through interactions with the amygdala.
source: The medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) plays a central role in social behavior (Duncan and Owen, 2000; Wood and Grafman, 2003; Bicks et al., 2015) through functional interactions with the amygdala (Kumar et al., 2014; Adhikari et al., 2015; Bukalo et al., 2015; Tovote et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to studies demonstrating mPFC-amygdala interactions

claim: The amygdala is reciprocally connected with the mPFC.
source: a region that is reciprocally connected with the mPFC (Vertes, 2004; Hoover and Vertes, 2007; Adhikari et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to anatomical studies

claim: The amygdala plays central roles in emotional responses such as fear and anxiety.
source: a region that is reciprocally connected with the mPFC (Vertes, 2004; Hoover and Vertes, 2007; Adhikari et al., 2015) and plays central roles in emotional responses such as fear and anxiety.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge and citations

claim: A number of gene expression patterns and intracellular signaling pathways related to social behavior have been identified in the mPFC.
source: A number of gene expression patterns and intracellular signaling pathways related to social behavior have been identified in the mPFC (Bicks et al., 2015; Schubert et al., 2015; Yan and Rein, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Alterations in overall mPFC neuronal excitability have been reported in humans with psychiatric disorders with social behavior deficits such as autism spectrum disorders and depression.
source: Under pathological conditions, a number of studies have reported alterations in overall mPFC neuronal excitability and disruptions of mPFC-amygdala interactions in humans with psychiatric disorders with social behavior deficits such as autism spectrum disorders (ASD) and depression (Happé et al., 1996; Castelli et al., 2002; Pierce et al., 2004; Greicius et al., 2007; Drysdale et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to clinical studies

claim: Disruptions of mPFC-amygdala interactions have been reported in humans with psychiatric disorders with social behavior deficits such as autism spectrum disorders and depression.
source: Under pathological conditions, a number of studies have reported alterations in overall mPFC neuronal excitability and disruptions of mPFC-amygdala interactions in humans with psychiatric disorders with social behavior deficits such as autism spectrum disorders (ASD) and depression (Happé et al., 1996; Castelli et al., 2002; Pierce et al., 2004; Greicius et al., 2007; Drysdale et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to clinical studies

claim: Alterations in mPFC neuronal excitability and disruptions of mPFC-amygdala interactions have been reported in animal models of autism spectrum disorders and depression.
source: and animal models of these disorders (Brumback et al., 2018; Abe et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to animal model studies

claim: Local field potential signals consist of diverse oscillatory patterns that dynamically vary with attentional, motivational, arousal states, and entrain synchronous rhythmic spikes.
source: Neurophysiological signatures representing neuronal population activity are local field potential (LFP) signals, consisting of diverse oscillatory patterns that dynamically vary with attentional, motivational, arousal states, and entrain synchronous rhythmic spikes (Buzsáki, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to foundational work on LFP signals

claim: A PFC oscillation at a low gamma-range (20–50 Hz) band mediated by interneurons facilitates social interaction.
source: A PFC oscillation at a low gamma-range (20–50 Hz) band mediated by interneurons facilitates social interaction (Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Autism mouse models with social deficits exhibit impairments in PFC interneuronal activity.
source: Consistently, autism mouse models with social deficits exhibit impairments in PFC interneuronal activity (Han et al., 2012) and gamma oscillations (Cao et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on autism mouse models

claim: Autism mouse models with social deficits exhibit impairments in PFC gamma oscillations.
source: Consistently, autism mouse models with social deficits exhibit impairments in PFC interneuronal activity (Han et al., 2012) and gamma oscillations (Cao et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on autism mouse models

claim: Theta-range (4–12 Hz) LFP signals in the prefrontal-amygdalar circuit are associated with the expression of emotional behavior such as fear retrieval.
source: On the other hand, several studies have shown that theta-range (4–12 Hz) LFP signals in the prefrontal-amygdalar circuit are associated with the expression of emotional behavior (Calıskan and Stork, 2019) such as fear retrieval (Seidenbecher et al., 2003; Likhtik et al., 2014; Stujenske et al., 2014; Dejean et al., 2016; Karalis et al., 2016; Ozawa et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Theta-range (4–12 Hz) LFP signals in the prefrontal-amygdalar circuit are associated with anxiety.
source: and anxiety (Adhikari et al., 2010; Likhtik et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: mPFC LFP power at a theta frequency (2–7 Hz) band influences oscillatory activity in the amygdala and ventral tegmental area during stress experiences.
source: In addition, mPFC LFP power at a theta frequency (2–7 Hz) band influences oscillatory activity in the amygdala and ventral tegmental area during stress experiences (Hultman et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: mPFC LFP power at a theta frequency (2–7 Hz) band predicts vulnerability to mental stress in individual animals.
source: and predicts vulnerability to mental stress in individual animals (Kumar et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: The majority of wild-type mice (11 out of 14) exhibited SI ratios of more than 1.
source: Consistent with previous observations (Golden et al., 2011; Venzala et al., 2012; Ramaker and Dulawa, 2017), the majority of wild-type mice (11 out of 14) exhibited SI ratios of more than 1 (Figure 1B), demonstrating their motivation for social interactions.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and consistent with cited prior observations

claim: Wild-type mice with SI ratios of more than 1 demonstrate their motivation for social interactions.
source: Consistent with previous observations (Golden et al., 2011; Venzala et al., 2012; Ramaker and Dulawa, 2017), the majority of wild-type mice (11 out of 14) exhibited SI ratios of more than 1 (Figure 1B), demonstrating their motivation for social interactions.
evidence: Interpretation of SI ratio data based on established behavioral paradigm

claim: dmPFC 4–7 Hz power in the target session was significantly increased to 113.1 ± 4.0% compared with the no target session.
source: Overall, dmPFC 4–7 Hz and 30–60 Hz power in the target session was significantly increased to 113.1 ± 4.0% and decreased to 94.6 ± 1.6%, respectively (Figure 1F, n=14 mice, 4–7 Hz: t13=3.56, p=0.0070; 30–60 Hz: t13 = 2.99, p=0.021, paired t-test followed by Bonferroni correction)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental LFP data shown in Figure 1F

claim: dmPFC 30–60 Hz power in the target session was significantly decreased to 94.6 ± 1.6% compared with the no target session.
source: Overall, dmPFC 4–7 Hz and 30–60 Hz power in the target session was significantly increased to 113.1 ± 4.0% and decreased to 94.6 ± 1.6%, respectively (Figure 1F, n=14 mice, 4–7 Hz: t13=3.56, p=0.0070; 30–60 Hz: t13 = 2.99, p=0.021, paired t-test followed by Bonferroni correction)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental LFP data shown in Figure 1F

claim: BLA 4–7 Hz power in the target session was significantly increased to 110.6 ± 2.7% compared with the no target session.
source: and BLA 4–7 Hz was significantly increased to 110.6 ± 2.7%, compared with that in the no target session (Figure 1G, n=6 mice, 4–7 Hz: t5=4.95, p=0.0086; 30–60 Hz: t5 = 2.13, p=0.17, paired t-test followed by Bonferroni correction).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental LFP data shown in Figure 1G

claim: dmPFC-BLA 4–7 Hz and 30–60 Hz power specifically become higher and lower, respectively, when mice are exposed to an environment including the other target mouse.
source: These results suggest that dmPFC-BLA 4–7 Hz and 30–60 Hz power specifically become higher and lower, respectively, when mice are exposed to an environment including the other target mouse.
evidence: Inference drawn from the experimental data comparing target and no target sessions

claim: No pronounced phase-amplitude coupling was found between the 4–7 Hz and 30–60 Hz frequency bands in both the dmPFC and BLA LFP traces.
source: Unlike fear-related theta-gamma coupling reported previously (Stujenske et al., 2014), we found no pronounced phase-amplitude coupling between the 4–7 Hz and 30–60 Hz frequency bands in both the dmPFC and BLA LFP traces (a representative result shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by phase-amplitude coupling analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B

claim: dmPFC-BLA coherence at the 4–7 Hz band in the target session was significantly higher than that in the no target session.
source: In addition to the LFP power changes, dmPFC-BLA coherence at the 4–7 Hz band in the target session was significantly higher than that in the no target session (Figure 1H, n=6 mice, 4–7 Hz: t5=3.95, p=0.022; 30–60 Hz: t5 = 1.37, p=0.46, paired t-test followed by Bonferroni correction)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of coherence data shown in Figure 1H

claim: The granger causality index at the 4–7 Hz band for the direction from the dmPFC to BLA was significantly higher than that for the direction from the BLA to the dmPFC.
source: The granger causality spectrum exhibited a significantly higher granger causality index at the 4–7 Hz band for the direction from the dmPFC to BLA than that for the direction from the BLA to the dmPFC (Figure 1I, n=6 mice, 4–7 Hz: p=0.030; 30–60 Hz: p=0.26, Mann-Whitney U test followed by Bonferroni correction)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of granger causality data shown in Figure 1I

claim: The preferential granger causality from dmPFC to BLA possibly reflects the preferential projection of the dmPFC to the BLA.
source: possibly reflecting the preferential projection of the dmPFC to the BLA (Gabbott et al., 2005; Bukalo et al., 2015).
evidence: Inference based on granger causality data and supported by citations to anatomical studies

claim: No significant correlations were found between dmPFC LFP power changes in the target session and SI ratios in wild-type mice.
source: However, we found no significant correlations between these two variables (n=14 mice, 4–7 Hz: R = –0.27, p=0.34; 30–60 Hz: R=0.40, p=0.15)
evidence: Supported by statistical correlation analysis of experimental data

claim: Individual differences in social behavior are not crucially associated with dmPFC power changes at least within the wild-type mouse group.
source: demonstrating that individual differences in social behavior are not crucially associated with dmPFC power changes at least within the wild-type mouse group.
evidence: Inference drawn from the lack of correlation between SI ratios and dmPFC power changes

claim: Moving speed was significantly higher in the no target session than in the target session.
source: To test this possibility, we compared moving speed between the two sessions and found that moving speed was significantly higher in the no target session than in the target session (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D; Z=20.20, p=9.0 × 10-89, Mann-Whitney U test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D

claim: Both in the dmPFC and BLA, 4–7 Hz power during stop periods was significantly higher than that during running periods.
source: Both in the dmPFC and BLA, 4–7 Hz power during stop periods was significantly higher than that during running periods (dmPFC, Z=4.93, p=8.26 × 10–7; BLA, Z=2.42, p=0.016, Mann-Whitney U test)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of LFP power during different movement states

claim: 30–60 Hz power exhibited opposite changes to 4–7 Hz power between stop and running periods.
source: whereas 30–60 Hz power exhibited opposite changes (dmPFC, Z=2.13, p=0.033, p=0.19; BLA, Z=2.00, p=0.045)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of LFP power during different movement states

claim: Locomotion is a crucial factor to affect 4–7 Hz and 30–60 Hz LFP power changes.
source: suggesting that locomotion is a crucial factor to affect these LFP power changes.
evidence: Inference drawn from the differences in LFP power between running and stop periods

claim: Significant increases in dmPFC LFP power in the target session were observed during stop periods but not running periods.
source: Similar to Figure 1F, significant increases in dmPFC LFP power in the target session were observed during stop periods but not running periods (Figure 1—figure supplement 2H, stop periods: n=14 mice, 4–7 Hz: t13=3.72, p=0.0052; 30–60 Hz: t13 = 3.05, p=0.019; Figure 1—figure supplement 2G, running periods: 4–7 Hz: t13=1.33, p=0.41; 30–60 Hz: t13 = 1.25, p=0.46, paired t-test followed by Bonferroni correction).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of LFP power during stop and running periods shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2G and 2H

claim: dmPFC 4–7 Hz power in the target session with a C57BL/6J target mouse was significantly higher than that in the no target session.
source: Similar to the results when the target CD-1 mice were used (Figure 1F), dmPFC 4–7 Hz power in the target session was significantly higher than that in the no target session (Figure 1J, n=6 mice, 4–7 Hz: t5=5.36, p=0.0060; 30–60 Hz: t5 = 1.04, p=0.70, paired t-test followed by Bonferroni correction).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1J

claim: Significant changes in dmPFC 4–7 Hz and 30–60 Hz power between the two sessions were not observed when a plastic toy mouse was placed in the cage instead of a real mouse.
source: In this case, significant changes in dmPFC 4–7 Hz and 30–60 Hz power between the two sessions were not observed (Figure 1K, n=7 mice, 4–7 Hz: t6=0.51, p>0.99; 30–60 Hz: t6 = 0.60, p>0.99, paired t-test followed by Bonferroni correction).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of control experiment data shown in Figure 1K

claim: The dmPFC power changes are induced specifically in a condition where mice exhibit social behavior while they are less associated with an object novelty or emotional components such as anxiety.
source: These results further confirm that the dmPFC power changes are induced specifically in a condition where mice exhibit social behavior while they are less associated with an object novelty or emotional components such as anxiety.
evidence: Inference drawn from comparing results with real mice versus toy mouse

claim: No significant differences in dmPFC and BLA 4–7 Hz and 30–60 Hz LFP power were observed among avoidance zones, peripheral areas, and center area in the no target session.
source: In the no target session, no significant differences in dmPFC and BLA 4–7 Hz and 30–60 Hz LFP power were observed among these areas (Figure 2B, dmPFC: n=7 mice, 4–7 Hz, F2,40 = 1.36, p=0.27; 30–60 Hz; F2,40 = 0.11, p=0.90; Figure 2C, BLA: n=6 mice, 4–7 Hz, F2,16 = 1.12, p=0.35; 30–60 Hz; F2,16 = 0.61, p=0.56, one-way ANOVA).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of LFP power across different spatial zones shown in Figure 2B and 2C

claim: No significant differences in dmPFC and BLA 4–7 Hz and 30–60 Hz LFP power were observed among avoidance zones, peripheral areas, and center area in the target session.
source: In the target session, no significant differences in dmPFC and BLA 4–7 Hz and 30–60 Hz LFP power were observed among these areas (Figure 2B, dmPFC: n=14 mice, 4–7 Hz, F2,35 = 0.50, p=0.61; 30–60 Hz; F2,35 = 0.13, p=0.88; Figure 2C, BLA: n=6 mice, 4–7 Hz, F1,10 = 3.38, p=0.099; 30–60 Hz; F1,10 = 0.27, p=0.62, one-way ANOVA).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of LFP power across different spatial zones shown in Figure 2B and 2C

claim: Anxiety-related environments are not crucially associated with 4–7 Hz and 30–60 Hz LFP power changes in the dmPFC and BLA.
source: These results suggest that anxiety-related environments are not crucially associated with 4–7 Hz and 30–60 Hz LFP power changes in the dmPFC and BLA observed in this study.
evidence: Inference drawn from the lack of differences in LFP power across anxiety-related spatial zones

claim: The SI ratios in 7 Shank3 KO mice were significantly lower than those in the 14 wild-type mice.
source: The SI ratios in 7 Shank3 KO mice were significantly lower than those in the 14 wild-type mice (Figure 3A, Z=2.65, p=0.016, Mann-Whitney U test followed by Bonferroni correction).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Shank3 KO mice exhibited significant increases in dmPFC and BLA LFP power during the target session at the 4–7 Hz bands.
source: We recorded LFP signals from the dmPFC and BLA of these Shank3 KO mice and found significant increases in dmPFC and BLA LFP power during the target session at the 4–7 Hz bands, similar to the wild-type mice (Figure 3B, dmPFC: n=7 mice, 4–7 Hz, t6=6.04, p=1.8 × 10–3; 30–60 Hz; t6=2.62, p=0.078; Figure 3C, BLA: n=7 mice, 4–7 Hz, t6=3.03, p=0.048; 30–60 Hz; t6=3.52, p=0.026, paired t-test followed by Bonferroni correction).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of LFP data from Shank3 KO mice shown in Figure 3B and 3C

claim: The dmPFC 4–7 Hz increases during the target session in the Shank3 KO mice were significantly larger than those observed in the wild-type mice.
source: Moreover, the dmPFC 4–7 Hz increases during the target session in the Shank3 KO mice were significantly larger than those observed in the wild-type mice (Figure 3B, F2,24=4.21, p=0.027, one-way ANOVA across wild-type, Shank3 KO, and defeated mouse groups; Z=2.36, p=0.046, Mann-Whitney U test followed by Bonferroni correction)
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison between wild-type and Shank3 KO mice shown in Figure 3B

claim: The increases in dmPFC 4–7 Hz power during a target session are more prominent in Shank3 KO mice, compared with wild-type mice.
source: These results suggest that the increases in dmPFC 4–7 Hz power during a target session are more prominent in Shank3 KO mice, compared with wild-type mice.
evidence: Inference drawn from the statistical comparison of dmPFC 4–7 Hz power between wild-type and Shank3 KO mice

claim: Shank3 KO mice spent substantial (26.0 ± 6.8%) time in the avoidance zones during the target session.
source: During the target session, the Shank3 KO mice spent substantial (26.0 ± 6.8%) time in the avoidance zones (Figure 3A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: When Shank3 KO mice stayed within the avoidance zone, dmPFC 4–7 Hz was significantly increased, compared with the other areas.
source: When the Shank3 KO mice stayed within the avoidance zone, dmPFC 4–7 Hz was significantly increased, compared with the other areas (Figure 4B, dmPFC: n=7 mice, 4–7 Hz, t5=4.39, p=0.014; 30–60 Hz; t5=0.33, p>0.99; BLA: n=7 mice, 4–7 Hz, t5=1.62, p=0.32; 30–60 Hz; t5=0.17, p>0.99, paired t-test followed by Bonferroni correction).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of LFP power in avoidance zones shown in Figure 4B

claim: Wild-type mice did not show significant changes in dmPFC and BLA 4–7 Hz and 30–60 Hz power in avoidance zones compared to other areas.
source: Such significant changes were not observed in the wild-type mice (Figure 4A, dmPFC: n=13 mice that stayed in the avoidance zones, 4–7 Hz, t12=0.068, p>0.99; 30–60 Hz; t12=0.71, p=0.98; BLA: n=5 mice that stayed in the avoidance zones, 4–7 Hz, t4=0.49, p>0.99; 30–60 Hz; t4=0.27, p>0.99, paired t-test followed by Bonferroni correction).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of LFP power in avoidance zones shown in Figure 4A

claim: Shank3 KO mice specifically exhibit a dmPFC 4–7 Hz power increase during avoidance behavior.
source: These results demonstrate that Shank3 KO mice specifically exhibit a dmPFC 4–7 Hz power increase during avoidance behavior.
evidence: Inference drawn from the comparison of LFP power in avoidance zones between wild-type and Shank3 KO mice

claim: SI ratios of the 6 defeated mice were significantly lower than those in the 14 wild-type mice.
source: SI ratios of the 6 defeated mice were significantly lower than those in the 14 wild-type mice (Figure 3A; Z=4.10, p=8.1 × 10–5, Mann-Whitney U test followed by Bonferroni correction).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Defeated mice exhibited a significantly larger increase in dmPFC 4–7 Hz power during the target session than during the no target session.
source: Similar to the wild-type and Shank3 KO mice, these defeated mice exhibited a significantly larger increase in dmPFC 4–7 Hz power during the target session than during the no target session (Figure 3B, dmPFC: n=6 mice, 4–7 Hz, t5=6.93, p=9.6 × 10–4; 30–60 Hz; t5=3.77, p=0.013; BLA: n=5 mice, 4–7 Hz: t4=1.88, p=0.14; 30–60 Hz: t4=0.33, p=0.76).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of LFP data from defeated mice shown in Figure 3B

claim: The dmPFC 4–7 Hz increase in the defeated mice was significantly larger than that observed from the wild-type mice.
source: In addition, similar to the Shank3 KO mice, the dmPFC 4–7 Hz increase in the defeated mice was significantly larger than that observed from the wild-type mice (Figure 3B, dmPFC: 4–7 Hz: Z=2.27, p=0.046; 30–60 Hz: Z=1.36, p=0.34; Figure 3C, BLA: 4–7 Hz: p>0.99; 30–60 Hz: p=0.50, Mann-Whitney U test followed by Bonferroni correction).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison between wild-type and defeated mice shown in Figure 3B

claim: Defeated mice spent 54.7 ± 9.5% of an entire recording time in the avoidance zones.
source: Furthermore, defeated mice spent 54.7 ± 9.5% of an entire recording time in the avoidance zones (Figure 3A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: Defeated mice exhibited significant increases in dmPFC 4–7 Hz power in the avoidance zone.
source: and exhibited significant increases in dmPFC 4–7 Hz power in the avoidance zone (Figure 4C, dmPFC: n=6 mice, 4–7 Hz, t5=11.68, p=1.8 × 10–4; 30–60 Hz; t5=3.45, p=0.036; BLA: n=5 mice, 4–7 Hz, t4=0.47, p>0.99; 30–60 Hz; t4=0.46, p>0.99, paired t-test followed by Bonferroni correction).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of LFP power in avoidance zones shown in Figure 4C

claim: A dmPFC 4–7 Hz power increase during social avoidance also occurs in depression model mice, similar to Shank3 KO mice.
source: These results demonstrate that a dmPFC 4–7 Hz power increase during social avoidance also occurs in depression model mice, similar to Shank3 KO mice.
evidence: Inference drawn from the comparison of LFP power in avoidance zones between Shank3 KO and defeated mice

claim: dmPFC 4–7 Hz power increases during social avoidance behavior are a common hallmark across socially deficient mouse models.
source: Taken together, our results from the two mouse models suggest that dmPFC 4–7 Hz power increases during social avoidance behavior are a common hallmark across socially deficient mouse models.
evidence: Inference drawn from the consistent findings across Shank3 KO and defeated mice

claim: No significant changes in 4–7 Hz and 30–60 Hz power in the dmPFC and BLA during the target session were detected between the IZ and the other areas.
source: However, no significant changes in 4–7 Hz and 30–60 Hz power in the dmPFC and BLA during the target session were detected between the IZ and the other areas (Figure 5—figure supplement 1; dmPFC, n=14 mice; 4–7 Hz: t13 = 0.76, p=0.46; 30–60 Hz: t13 = 1.38, p=0.19; BLA, n=6 mice; 4–7 Hz: t5 = 0.76, p=0.48; 30–60 Hz: t5 = 0.02, p=0.98, paired t-test followed by Bonferroni correction).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of LFP power in IZ versus other areas shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Animals' motivation toward and salience regarding the other mouse are not equivalent even when they are similarly located in an IZ.
source: These behavioral observations indicate that animals' motivation toward and salience regarding the other mouse are not equivalent even when they are similarly located in an IZ.
evidence: Inference drawn from behavioral observations of variable behavior patterns within the IZ

claim: Changes in dmPFC-BLA oscillations are not simply explained by where the mice stayed in the SI test.
source: The results suggest that changes in dmPFC-BLA oscillations are not simply explained by where the mice stayed in the SI test.
evidence: Inference drawn from the lack of LFP power differences between IZ and other areas

claim: No significant differences in the distributions of moving speed were found between the approach behavior and leaving behavior.
source: No significant differences in the distributions of moving speed were found between the approach behavior and leaving behavior (Figure 5D; Z=0.85, p=0.39, Mann-Whitney U test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of moving speed shown in Figure 5D

claim: Approach and leaving behavior is not explained by speed or locomotion itself.
source: These results confirm that approach and leaving behavior is not explained by speed or locomotion itself, allowing us to compare LFP power between the two behavioral periods without being affected by moving speed.
evidence: Inference drawn from the lack of speed differences between approach and leaving behavior

claim: Both in the dmPFC and BLA, 4–7 Hz power was significantly decreased during the approach behavior compared with the leaving behavior.
source: Both in the dmPFC and BLA, 4–7 Hz power was significantly decreased during the approach behavior compared with the leaving behavior (Figure 5F, left, dmPFC: 4–7 Hz: t13=2.71, p=0.018; 30–60 Hz: t13=0.47, p=0.65; Figure 5F, middle, BLA: 4–7 Hz: t5=2.83, p=0.037; 30–60 Hz: t5=1.01, p=0.36, paired t-test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of LFP power during approach versus leaving behavior shown in Figure 5F

claim: dmPFC-BLA coherence at the 4–7 Hz band during leaving behavior was significantly higher than that during approach behavior.
source: Consistent with the LFP power changes, dmPFC-BLA coherence at the 4–7 Hz band during leaving behavior was significantly higher than that during approach behavior (Figure 5F, right, n=6 mice, 4–7 Hz: t5=6.34, p=0.0028; 30–60 Hz: t5 = 5.54, p=0.0052, paired t-test followed by Bonferroni correction).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of coherence during approach versus leaving behavior shown in Figure 5F

claim: The Granger causality index at the 4–7 Hz band in the dmPFC-BLA direction was significantly higher than that in the BLA-dmPFC direction during leaving behavior, but not during approach behavior.
source: Moreover, the Granger causality index at the 4–7 Hz band in the dmPFC-BLA direction was significantly higher than that in the BLA-dmPFC direction during leaving behavior, but not during approach behavior (Figure 5G, n=6 mice, 4–7 Hz: p=0.030; 30–60 Hz: p=0.26, Mann-Whitney U test followed by Bonferroni correction).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of Granger causality during approach versus leaving behavior shown in Figure 5G

claim: Functional information transfer at the 4–7 Hz band from the dmPFC to the BLA is lowered during social approach behavior, compared with leaving behavior.
source: These results suggest that functional information transfer at the 4–7 Hz band from the dmPFC to the BLA is lowered during social approach behavior, compared with leaving behavior.
evidence: Inference drawn from the Granger causality analysis during approach versus leaving behavior

claim: Shank3 KO mice did not show significant differences in dmPFC 4–7 Hz and 30–60 Hz power between approach and leaving behavior.
source: In Shank3 KO mice, we did not observe significant differences in dmPFC 4–7 Hz and 30–60 Hz power between approach and leaving behavior (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, n=7 mice, 4–7 Hz: t6=0.48, p=0.65; 30–60 Hz: t6=0.67, p=0.53, paired t-test followed by Bonferroni correction)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of LFP power during approach versus leaving behavior in Shank3 KO mice shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D

claim: Social behavior-related dmPFC activity is not properly regulated in socially deficient mice.
source: suggesting that social behavior-related dmPFC activity is not properly regulated in socially deficient mice.
evidence: Inference drawn from the lack of LFP power differences between approach and leaving behavior in Shank3 KO mice

claim: The reductions of dmPFC 4–7 Hz power during social interaction behavior are consistent with the opposite changes (the increases in dmPFC 4–7 Hz power) observed during social avoidance behavior in the socially deficient mice.
source: The reductions of dmPFC 4–7 Hz power during social interaction behavior are consistent with the opposite changes (the increases in dmPFC 4–7 Hz power) observed during social avoidance behavior in the socially deficient mice (shown in Figures 3 and 4).
evidence: Inference drawn from comparing LFP power changes during approach behavior and avoidance behavior

claim: Changes in dmPFC 4–7 Hz oscillations are a key neuronal substrate to modulate social behavior and social avoidance.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that changes in dmPFC 4–7 Hz oscillations are a key neuronal substrate to modulate social behavior and social avoidance.
evidence: Inference drawn from the consistent findings across multiple experiments and mouse models

claim: Putative regular-spiking (RS) excitatory pyramidal neurons were identified as neurons that had baseline spike rates lower than 10 Hz and spike widths longer than 0.6ms.
source: Following the criteria utilized in previous studies (Wilson et al., 1994; Tierney et al., 2004; Homayoun and Moghaddam, 2007), as shown in Figure 6A, putative regular-spiking (RS) excitatory pyramidal neurons were identified as neurons that had baseline spike rates lower than 10 Hz and spike widths longer than 0.6ms (n=48 neurons from 11 mice).
evidence: Based on established classification criteria from cited prior studies

claim: Putative fast-spiking (FS) interneurons were identified as neurons that had baseline spike rates higher than 10 Hz.
source: On the other hand, putative fast-spiking (FS) interneurons were identified as neurons that had baseline spike rates higher than 10 Hz (n=9 neurons from 6 mice).
evidence: Based on established classification criteria from cited prior studies

claim: The remaining FS neurons showed significantly higher MVL for the 4–7 Hz oscillations during leaving periods, compared with approach periods.
source: After this exclusion, the remaining FS neurons showed significantly higher MVL for the 4–7 Hz oscillations during leaving periods, compared with approach periods (n=6 neurons; t5=3.15, p=0.025, paired t-test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of MVL during approach versus leaving behavior

claim: A subset of FS neurons alter their entrainment to the 4–7 Hz oscillations depending on animal's behavioral patterns.
source: These results demonstrate that a subset of FS neurons alter their entrainment to the 4–7 Hz oscillations depending on animal's behavioral patterns.
evidence: Inference drawn from the MVL analysis showing behavior-dependent changes

claim: mPFC FS neurons are more preferentially entrained by the 4–7 Hz oscillations during leaving behavior than approach behavior.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that mPFC FS neurons are more preferentially entrained by the 4–7 Hz oscillations during leaving behavior than approach behavior.
evidence: Inference drawn from the MVL analysis showing higher entrainment during leaving behavior

claim: The entrainment of mPFC neurons to the 4–7 Hz oscillations is disrupted when mice engage in social approach behavior.
source: In other words, the entrainment of mPFC neurons to the 4–7 Hz oscillations is disrupted when mice engage in social approach behavior.
evidence: Inference drawn from the MVL analysis showing lower entrainment during approach behavior

claim: Photostimulation at 4 Hz induced a significant 19.5 ± 9.0% power increase in the corresponding frequency (4–7 Hz) band in the dmPFC.
source: Photostimulation at 4 Hz induced a significant 19.5 ± 9.0% power increase in the corresponding frequency (4–7 Hz) band in the dmPFC (Figure 7B and C; 4–7 Hz: t15=2.44, p=0.045; 30–60 Hz: t15=2.18, p=0.066, paired t-test)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of LFP power changes during optogenetic stimulation shown in Figure 7B and C

claim: Photostimulation at 40 Hz induced significant 24.8 ± 14.1% and 2.8 ± 0.9% power increases at the corresponding frequency (30–60 Hz) band in the dmPFC and BLA, respectively.
source: Photostimulation at 40 Hz induced significant 24.8 ± 14.1% and 2.8 ± 0.9% power increases at the corresponding frequency (30–60 Hz) band in the dmPFC and BLA, respectively (Figure 7B and C, dmPFC: t15=2.91, p=0.023; BLA: t15=3.27, p=0.017).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of LFP power changes during optogenetic stimulation shown in Figure 7B and C

claim: The 40 Hz photostimulation induced significant 17.5 ± 5.4% and 6.4 ± 2.6% power decreases in the 4–7 Hz band in the dmPFC and BLA, respectively.
source: In addition, the 40 Hz photostimulation induced significant 17.5 ± 5.4% and 6.4 ± 2.6% power decreases in the 4–7 Hz band in the dmPFC and BLA, respectively (Figure 7C, dmPFC: t15=3.24, p=0.014; BLA: t15=2.49, p=0.047).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of LFP power changes during optogenetic stimulation shown in Figure 7C

claim: The bidirectional changes in 4–7 Hz and 30–60 Hz power in the dmPFC-BLA circuit at 40 Hz photostimulation are consistent with those observed during social approach behavior.
source: The bidirectional changes in 4–7 Hz and 30–60 Hz power in the dmPFC-BLA circuit at 40 Hz photostimulation are consistent with those observed during social approach behavior, as shown in Figure 5, suggesting that it was possible to replicate social interaction-related neuronal activity.
evidence: Inference drawn from comparing optogenetic stimulation effects with natural behavior-related LFP changes

claim: In the mice expressing ChR2-YFP, 40 Hz photostimulation significantly increased occupancy time in the IZ, compared with no photostimulation.
source: In the mice expressing ChR2-YFP, 40 Hz photostimulation significantly increased occupancy time in the IZ, compared with no photostimulation (Figure 7F; n=7 mice; t6 = 3.46, p=0.040, paired t-test followed by Bonferroni correction)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data during optogenetic stimulation shown in Figure 7F

claim: No significant changes in IZ occupancy were observed by 4 Hz and 10 Hz photostimulation in mice expressing ChR2-YFP.
source: whereas no significant changes were observed by 4 Hz and 10 Hz photostimulation (4 Hz: t6=0.56, p>0.99; 10 Hz: t6=0.25, p>0.99, paired t-test followed by Bonferroni correction).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data during optogenetic stimulation

claim: In the mice expressing YFP alone, no significant effects on IZ occupancy were observed in any photostimulation conditions.
source: On the other hand, in the mice expressing YFP alone, no significant effects were observed in any photostimulation conditions (Figure 7G; n=5 mice; 4 Hz: t4=2.05, p=0.87; 10 Hz: t4=2.16, p=0.83; 40 Hz: t4=2.51, p=0.72, paired t-test followed by Bonferroni correction).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of control experiment data shown in Figure 7G

claim: Optogenetic inductions of a decrease in dmPFC-BLA 4–7 Hz power and an increase in 30–60 Hz power are sufficient to trigger social interaction behavior.
source: Overall, these results demonstrate that optogenetic inductions of a decrease in dmPFC-BLA 4–7 Hz power and an increase in 30–60 Hz power are sufficient to trigger social interaction behavior.
evidence: Inference drawn from the optogenetic experiments showing increased IZ occupancy with 40 Hz stimulation

claim: All mouse types tested exhibited prominent increases in dmPFC-BLA 4–7 Hz power and decreases in 30–60 Hz power throughout a target session compared with a no target session.
source: Power spectrum analyses revealed that all mouse types tested exhibited prominent increases in dmPFC-BLA 4–7 Hz power and decreases in 30–60 Hz power throughout a target session compared with a no target session.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings across all mouse groups

claim: The dmPFC 4–7 Hz power increase was prominent when socially deficient mouse models exhibited social avoidance behavior.
source: The dmPFC 4–7 Hz power increase was prominent when socially deficient mouse models exhibited social avoidance behavior.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings in Shank3 KO and defeated mice

claim: dmPFC 4–7 Hz power was dynamically reduced when wild-type mice exhibited social approach behavior compared with leaving behavior with opposite moving directions.
source: In contrast, dmPFC 4–7 Hz power was dynamically reduced when wild-type mice exhibited social approach behavior compared with leaving behavior with opposite moving directions.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings during approach versus leaving behavior

claim: Replicating the social interaction-related LFP changes by oscillation-like optogenetic stimulation of PV interneurons was sufficient to increase social interaction in socially defeated mice.
source: Replicating the social interaction-related LFP changes by oscillation-like optogenetic stimulation of PV interneurons was sufficient to increase social interaction in socially defeated mice.
evidence: Summary of optogenetic experimental findings

claim: PV interneurons are a crucial cell type for generating cortical low gamma-range (20–60 Hz) oscillations.
source: Many previous studies have established that PV interneurons are a crucial cell type for generating cortical low gamma-range (20–60 Hz) oscillations (Whittington et al., 1995; Bartos et al., 2007; Cardin et al., 2009; Sohal et al., 2009; Buzsáki and Wang, 2012; Nakamura et al., 2015; Cao et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: The PV-interneuron-mediated gamma oscillation in the PFC is enhanced during social interaction.
source: The PV-interneuron-mediated gamma oscillation in the PFC is enhanced during social interaction (Liu et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: The PV-interneuron-mediated gamma oscillation in the PFC is attenuated in autism mouse models with social deficits.
source: or attenuated in autism mouse models with social deficits (Cao et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: PFC PV interneurons are important in the expression of social behavior through the regulation of low gamma oscillations.
source: highlighting the importance of PFC PV interneurons in the expression of social behavior (Han et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2019) through the regulation of low gamma oscillations (Cao et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: 40 Hz photostimulation selective to PV interneurons resulted in a decrease in dmPFC 4–7 Hz and an increase in 40 Hz power.
source: Notably, in our study, we initially sought to determine a protocol that could reduce dmPFC 4–7 Hz power to mimic the LFP power changes observed during approach behavior and eventually found that 40 Hz photostimulation selective to PV interneurons was optimal to meet this technical requirement, resulting in a decrease in dmPFC 4–7 Hz and an increase in 40 Hz power.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from optogenetic experiments

claim: The mechanisms underlying reciprocal power changes between 4–7 Hz and 40 Hz are possibly mediated by a stimulation-induced interference of the entrainment of PV interneuronal spikes by a 4–7 Hz oscillation.
source: The mechanisms underlying these reciprocal power changes are possibly mediated by a stimulation-induced interference of the entrainment of PV interneuronal spikes by a 4–7 Hz oscillation.
evidence: Speculative explanation for the observed optogenetic effects

claim: Optogenetic manipulations of PV interneurons extend to the BLA circuit.
source: Our study demonstrated that such optogenetic manipulations of PV interneurons extend to the BLA circuit
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing LFP power changes in BLA during dmPFC stimulation

claim: Optogenetic manipulations of PV interneurons were sufficient to restore social interaction behavior that was reduced in social defeat stress-induced depression mouse models.
source: and were sufficient to restore social interaction behavior that was reduced in social defeat stress-induced depression mouse models, similar to autism mouse models reported previously (Cao et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from optogenetic behavioral experiments and comparison with cited prior work

claim: Disruptions in E/I balances are crucial factors contributing to social behavior deficits in autism-like mouse models.
source: Accumulating evidence suggests that disruptions in E/I balances are crucial factors contributing to social behavior deficits in autism-like mouse models (Rubenstein and Merzenich, 2003; Helmeke et al., 2008; Yizhar et al., 2011; Selimbeyoglu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Dynamic changes in LFP oscillatory power regulated by inhibitory neuronal networks at appropriate timings are crucial for social behavior.
source: From the aspect of neuronal networks, our results add to a growing body of evidence demonstrating that dynamic changes in LFP oscillatory power regulated by inhibitory neuronal networks at appropriate timings are crucial for social behavior.
evidence: Inference drawn from the experimental findings in this study
